entities.name: Ulrich von Seckau
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ulrich of Seckau, a pivotal figure in the tumultuous ecclesiastical landscape of mid-13th century Central Europe, served as Bishop of Seckau before his contested election as Archbishop of Salzburg in 1257. His archiepiscopacy, which officially concluded in 1265, was defined by an unrelenting power struggle with Philip of Spanheim, the chosen candidate of King Ottokar II of Bohemia and a powerful secular prince. This prolonged dispute effectively paralyzed the Archdiocese of Salzburg, a vast and strategically important ecclesiastical principality within the Holy Roman Empire, hindering its administrative and spiritual functions during a period of imperial interregnum and regional consolidation of power in the Alpine region.

Elected by a segment of the Salzburg chapter following the death of Archbishop Bernhard von Zedersee, Ulrich immediately faced opposition from Philip of Spanheim, who had previously occupied the see as administrator and was supported by powerful secular interests, including his brother Duke Bernhard of Carinthia and King Ottokar II. Despite receiving papal confirmation from Pope Alexander IV, Ulrich was unable to assert full control over the archdiocese, which was largely held by Philip and his allies. The conflict escalated into military confrontations and political maneuvering, forcing Ulrich to often reside outside Salzburg and rely on the support of other regional powers, notably Duke Henry XIII of Bavaria. His tenure saw significant fragmentation of authority and resources within the archdiocese, as various factions vied for control, with churches and monasteries often caught in the middle.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ulrich von Seckau's contested archiepiscopacy was a microcosm of the power struggles during the Great Interregnum, significantly weakening the regional authority of the Archbishopric of Salzburg for nearly a decade and allowing secular rulers to expand their influence.
